title: Table Builder
context: Grade 4, and the page prints six empty tables rather than six filled ones. An adult sees rote learning. What the page is actually doing is asking for the tables to be built by repeated addition, which is a different thing from being told them, and then asking for the patterns that fall out. Those patterns are the part that survives: a child who knows the table of twelve is the table of six doubled can rebuild any row they have forgotten.

writeup.why: Build the tables past ten by adding rather than by remembering, and find the patterns that let you rebuild any row you forget.
writeup.look: An empty table of ten rows with only its first row written in, a running count down the side and a rail below that holds two tables level.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Table Builder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the rows filled against the rows the table is ruled for, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each row is added and the second fixed at the length of the table. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The table stands down the left of the working area, 360 by 528 at 64,202: ten rows 48 tall, each ruled into a row count at its left in a narrow band 72 wide and a product cell 288 wide beside it, with only the top product cell written in when the mount comes up. There is no lookup control anywhere on this stage. The only control that fills a row is add a row, and it draws the addition as a visible step: an arrow leaves the product above, the table's own number is written on the arrow itself, and the new product lands in the cell below. The running count strip runs down the far side of the table at 432,202, 56 wide, and each of its marks lands level with the row it counts, so the number of times taken and the row it made stay tied together and neither can be read without the other. The compare rail opens to the right of the table, 560 by 528 at 508,202, holding a second finished table with its rows level with the first and a clear channel 64 wide between the two columns of products. Light a pair lights the two products standing at one level, writes what links them in the channel between, and moves a row at a time under a finger drawn down the rail. The even check opens under whichever table is finished, 1086 by 132 at 64,608, as two trays marked odd and even with the last digit of every product lit on the table above; a product dropped into the wrong tray is pushed straight back out and returns to its row rather than being cleared. The steps counter takes the place of the compare rail when it is open, 560 by 528 at 508,202, and works one product twice in two columns standing side by side, once with the table open so that each column of the multiplicand is one fact from it, and once with the multiplier split into a ones row and a tens row in rose that are then added, with every line of writing numbered down its own margin and the two totals of those margins written at the foot. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a row, a product or a count of steps is asked for, and on the second and third phases a choice pad holding the tables themselves and the words odd and even, so that a table can be brought onto the rail and a last digit sorted with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product standing under the rule is green; a digit carried into the next column is vermilion and is always drawn small and inside a ring set above the column it is joining, never in the margin and never under the rule; a partial product row made by one place of the multiplier is rose; and a zero that is only holding a place open, or a step that is skipped, is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a carried digit by being small and by sitting in a ring above the column it is going into.
writeup.finish: The card shows the table the child built, its rows still numbered, standing beside whichever table it doubles.

phases.win: the table fills from the top and the running count keeps pace with the rows
phases.does: adds the number again for each row and watches the column fill downwards
phases.goal: every row of a table is the row above with the same number added once more
phases.says: Add the same number once more for every row. Never look a row up.
phases.check: The table of fifteen has 45 in its third row. Build the fourth and the fifth rows without looking anything up.
phases.feels: slow, and every row arrives out of the one above it rather than out of memory
phases.hands: Give each child a long paper strip and one number between eleven and sixteen. Write the number at the top and build every row under it by adding, never by recalling, saying the running count out loud as each row lands. Time how long the strip takes and keep it pinned up for the next session.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which number is this table built on? Second rung, the phase's: what is added to the row above to make the next one? Third rung: the table is cut to three rows and the child builds those three by adding, with the arrow drawn for the first of them. The number pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: two numbers run down a table, the row count and the products, and the one nearest the hand is the one that has just changed.
wrong.move: adds the row count to the row above instead of the table's own number, so that the table of fourteen runs 14, then 16, then 19.
wrong.screen: the row the child filled is emptied and the step is drawn again as an arrow off the row above it, with the table's own number written on the arrow itself, and the row count is moved out to the far side of the strip where it cannot be reached by accident. The child's row is redrawn faintly beside the rebuilt one so the two can be read together.

wrong.why: the early rows of any table are old ground, and a tool that fills one row at a time looks slow when the answer is already in the head.
wrong.move: asks for the rest of the table to be filled in at once, because the first few rows are already known by heart.
wrong.screen: the rows the child already holds stay filled exactly as they were given, and the steps between them are drawn in afterwards, each arrow carrying the table's own number, so that the rows known by heart are seen to be the same additions. The tool then stops at the first row the child did not have, with only the arrow off the row above it offered.

phases.screen: an empty table of ten rows with the number itself in the first row and no lookup anywhere
phases.soWhat: Build a table by adding the same number once more for every row.
phases.concept: A table is repeated addition written down

phases.win: every pair of rows lights as a double and the rail names the pattern
phases.does: reads the two rows that sit level and says how the one on the right was made
phases.goal: the table of twelve is the table of six doubled, and sixteen is eight doubled
phases.says: Read the two rows that sit level with each other. What has happened to the one on the left?
phases.check: 8 x 7 = 56. What is 16 x 7, and what did you do to 56 to get there?
phases.feels: a whole table arrives without a single row of it being added
phases.hands: Pin two finished paper strips side by side on the wall, the table of six and the table of twelve, with their rows level. Read the two products that sit level and ask what has happened to the one on the left. Then do the same with the table of eight and the table of sixteen, and ask whether it is the same thing happening twice.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is the smaller table built on? Second rung, the phase's: what has been done to that number to make the other one? Third rung: the rail is cut to three rows of each table and the child reads the three level pairs in turn. The choice pad stays open.

wrong.why: adding is what built the table in the first place, so adding is the move already in the hand, and adding six to a row of six is a true step in that table even though it is the wrong one here.
wrong.move: adds the smaller table's number to its product instead of doubling it, so that 42 in the table of six is read as 48 rather than 84.
wrong.screen: the two products standing level are lit together and read out, and the arrow between them is drawn as a second copy of the left hand product landing on top of itself rather than as a step along the table. The child's answer stays in the slot while the rail counts both readings out and shows which row of the table of six 48 actually is.

wrong.why: two things standing level look as though both of them have to be changed, and the row count is sitting right there in the same movement of the hand.
wrong.move: doubles the row count as well as the product and reads the answer off the wrong row.
wrong.screen: the row counts of the two tables are drawn out to the far edges of the rail and held still while the products alone are lit, and a finger drawn down the channel shows the one row count standing beside both tables at every level. The row the child read from is left lit in amber beside the row they were sent to.

phases.screen: the compare rail holding two finished tables side by side with their rows level
phases.soWhat: The table of twelve is the table of six doubled, and the table of sixteen is the table of eight doubled, row for row.
phases.concept: One table can be built from another

phases.win: every product lands in the even tray and an odd answer dropped in is pushed straight back out
phases.does: reads the last digit of every product and sorts them into odd and even
phases.goal: a table built on an even number has every product even
phases.says: Look at the last digit of every answer. Could any of them be odd?
phases.check: Someone says 14 x 7 comes to 99. What is wrong with that before any working is looked at, and what is the real product?
phases.feels: the last digit on its own says whether an answer could possibly belong to this table
phases.hands: Read the last digit of every product on a finished strip out loud and nothing else, so that the products themselves are never said. Do it once with a table built on an even number and once with a table built on an odd one, and ask what is different about the two lists.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the last digit of the answer that was given? Second rung, the phase's: what must the last digit of any product in this table be? Third rung: the check is cut to the first three products of the table and the child sorts those three. The choice pad of odd and even stays open.

wrong.why: the row count is the number that keeps changing, so it looks like the one that decides, and odd taken odd times has come out odd before now.
wrong.move: sorts by the multiplier rather than by the product, so an odd row count sends an even answer into the odd tray.
wrong.screen: the row counts are covered over on the strip and only the products are left standing, each with its last digit lit, and the products are then offered to the trays one at a time with nothing else in view. The child's earlier sorting is left drawn faintly under the tray it went into, and 16 x 9 is worked out in the open beside it as 144.

wrong.why: a rule that held for the last table looks like a rule about tables, and the even tray has been the right answer every time so far.
wrong.move: carries the rule across to a table built on an odd number and pushes every odd product in it back out.
wrong.screen: the odd table is stood beside the even one on the rail with both sets of last digits lit, and the two lists are read down together, so the odd table is heard running odd, even, odd, even while the even table does not change at all. The products the child pushed back are returned to the rows they came from.

phases.screen: a finished table with the even check open beneath it and two empty trays
phases.soWhat: Every product of a table built on an even number is even, so an odd answer there is wrong with no checking at all.
phases.concept: An even number gives an even product

phases.win: the table side finishes in fewer steps and both sides land on the same product
phases.does: works it both ways and counts the steps each route took
phases.goal: a table past ten turns a two digit multiplier into one fact for each column
phases.says: Count the steps each way took. Which of them would you rather write out?
phases.check: Find 507 x 12 using the table of twelve, and say how many column steps it took.
phases.feels: the same answer twice, and one of the two routes took noticeably less writing
phases.hands: Work 412 x 13 twice on paper. Once with the table of thirteen open, taking one fact from it for each column of 412. Once with the multiplier split into a ones row and a tens row that are then added. Both should come to 5356. Count the lines of writing each way took, and count the addition at the end as a line like any other.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many columns does the multiplicand have? Second rung, the phase's: how many facts does the table hand you for each of those columns? Third rung: the counter is cut to a two digit multiplicand and the child works both routes on that. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: every multiplier up to now has been one digit long, and two digits sitting side by side look like two of those, to be used one after the other.
wrong.move: uses the 1 and the 3 of the multiplier as two separate single digit multipliers and multiplies by each of them in turn.
wrong.screen: the multiplier is drawn out as its places, the tens part written in full as 10 and the ones part as 3, so that the 13 is seen to be one number made of a ten and a three and not two multipliers at all. Both routes are then worked side by side, the child's and the table's, and the first column where the two part is lit amber and stays lit.

wrong.why: the multiplying feels like the work and the adding at the end feels like tidying up afterwards, so it slips out of the count without being decided against.
wrong.move: counts the steps of the two routes but counts the adding of the two rows as no step at all.
wrong.screen: the two routes stand side by side with every line of writing numbered down its own margin, the addition of the two rows numbered like any other line, and the total of each margin written at its foot. The child's count stays exactly where it was written, beside the one the counter made.

phases.screen: the same product worked twice, once with the table open and once with the multiplier split
phases.soWhat: A table past ten turns a two digit multiplier into one fact for each column, instead of two rows that then have to be added.
phases.concept: A bigger table means fewer steps

writeup.delight: The second phase, the first time the compare rail brings a second table alongside. The two tables do not slide into place past one another. The rail lifts the rows of the table already standing and threads the new table's rows in between them, so that for a moment every row of six has a row of twelve resting on it. Then they separate into two columns with their rows dead level, and a finger drawn down the channel between them lights one level pair after another, each pair reading itself out as a number and its double. Draw the finger back up the rail and the pairs unlight in the same order they came.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase an empty table of ten numbered rows stands on the canvas with only its own number written into the top row, and there is no lookup anywhere on the bench to fill the rest of it from. On the second two finished tables stand on the compare rail with their rows dead level and no pair lit yet. On the third a finished table stands with the even check open beneath it and two empty trays waiting below that. On the fourth one product is set out twice, once beside an open table past ten and once with its multiplier split into a ones row and a tens row, and neither route has been worked. The running count at the top left holds the rows filled against the rows the table is ruled for, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the empty row under the number, or the first level pair, or the even tray, or the shorter of the two routes, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks for the next row. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any table from eleven to sixteen built by adding, the compare rail holding any two of them, and the even check open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on building a table by adding, reading one table off another, checking an even product and using a table past ten.
voiceLines: An empty table, and one number written into its top row. Every row after it is made by adding.
Add the same number once more for every row. Never look a row up.
Read the two rows that sit level with each other. What has happened to the one on the left?
Look at the last digit of every answer. Could any of them be odd?
Count the steps each way took. Which of them would you rather write out?
Another table to build. There is nothing in this tool to look a row up in.
Free play. Any table past ten, with the compare rail and the even check open.
Empty that row and build it again as a step off the row above it.
You built every row by adding, and then read a whole table straight off another one.

observations.why: Taking a number one more time is that number added once more, so the row count and the number of times taken are one count, not two.
observations.soWhat: A row you cannot remember can be rebuilt from the row beside it instead of waited for.
observations.observe: Every row of the table was the row above it with the same number added, and the count down the side went up by one each time.

observations.why: Twelve is six taken twice, so taking twelve any number of times is taking six that many times and then doubling what comes out.
observations.soWhat: A whole table can be read off a table already held, which is why the table of sixteen costs nothing once the table of eight is in.
observations.observe: With the table of six standing beside the table of twelve, every product on the right was the product level with it on the left, doubled.

observations.why: An even number is made of twos and stays made of twos however many times it is taken, while an odd number only comes out even when it is taken an even number of times.
observations.soWhat: An odd answer claimed for a table built on an even number is wrong before any working is looked at.
observations.observe: Every product in the table of fourteen ended in an even digit, while the table of fifteen ran odd, even, odd, even all the way down.

observations.why: A table past ten makes a two digit multiplier one fact for each column of the multiplicand, instead of two rows of its own that are each worked in full and then added.
observations.soWhat: A table learnt past ten is a shorter piece of writing every time it is used.
observations.observe: 412 x 13 took three column steps with the table of thirteen open, and more than that when the multiplier was split into a ones row and a tens row that then had to be added.

serves.exercise: recalling the multiplication tables to write the six answers
finding the missing number in each of the six given multiplications

source_tool.description: An empty table of ten rows stands on the stage with only the number itself written into the first row. There is no lookup anywhere in this tool: the only way a row fills is by adding the table's own number to the row above it, and the addition is drawn each time as a small step off the previous total. A strip along the side keeps the running count of how many times the number has been taken, so the row number and the repeated addition stay tied together. A compare rail opens beneath, holding two finished tables side by side with their rows level, and lighting a pair of rows at a time: the table of twelve against the table of six, and the table of sixteen against the table of eight, which are the two patterns the page names. An even product check opens under any finished table and sorts every product by its last digit, refusing an odd answer dropped into the even tray when the table was built on an even number. A steps counter runs one product two ways, once using a table past ten and once by splitting the multiplier, and counts the steps each route took.
source_tool.art_direction: An empty table filled by adding / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.note: THERE IS NO MODE AXIS ON THIS TOOL FAMILY. learn, practice and freeplay are gone and are not replaced by three of anything else: the axis itself is wrong for a tool a child works alone. See phase_mount.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, place cards that split off a multiplier, trays that hold a number while it is taken several times, a table strip that grows a row at a time, and a ruled grid with a diagonal in every cell.

A multiplication set out in columns always shows its columns: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the rows aligned by their right ends, and a horizontal rule between the last row and the product. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach multiplying.
A carried digit is always drawn small, inside a ring above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
A partial product row is drawn with the place of the multiplier that made it named beside it, and with its trailing zeros written rather than implied.

A lattice is drawn as a true grid of equal square cells with one straight diagonal in every cell, all running the same way, the digits of the two numbers sitting outside the grid, and every cell holding two digits on either side of its diagonal even when the pair multiplies to less than ten, so that nothing has to be carried while multiplying.
Where tokens or groups stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn, every group holds the same count, they never overlap, and they stay countable at a glance.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column, a cell or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A digit carried into the next column is vermilion, so it is told apart from the digits it is joining. A partial product row, made by one place of the multiplier, is rose, so a row is read as a part before it is read as an answer. A zero holding a place open, and a place of the multiplier that is skipped, are both grey, because neither one is a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carried digit is told apart by being small and sitting in a ring above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Empty that row and build it again as a step off the row above it.
voice.onNext: Another table to build. There is nothing in this tool to look a row up in.
voice.opening: An empty table, and one number written into its top row. Every row after it is made by adding.
voice.onFinish: You built every row by adding, and then read a whole table straight off another one.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any table past ten, with the compare rail and the even check open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A table is repeated addition written down
One table can be built from another
An even number gives an even product
A bigger table means fewer steps

placement.where: After the first table has been built on paper by adding, so the slowness has been felt. The tool is what stands two finished tables level with each other, which a page of six separate tables cannot.

answer_key.rule: A table is built by starting at the number itself and adding that same number once more for every row, so each row is one step further on than the row above. Every product in the table of twelve is double the product in the same row of the table of six, and every product in the table of sixteen is double the product in the same row of the table of eight. A table built on an even number has every product even, which catches an answer that cannot be right without any working. A table past ten turns a two digit multiplier into a single fact for each column of the multiplicand, instead of two rows that then have to be added together.
answer_key.wrong: The row is emptied and rebuilt as a step off the row above it, drawn slowly, with the running count lit beside it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The first row is the number itself, 14.
Each row after it is the row above with 14 added, so 14 + 14 = 28 and 28 + 14 = 42.
One more step gives 42 + 14 = 56, so the first four rows are 14, 28, 42 and 56.
items.question: Build the first four rows of the table of fourteen by repeated addition.
items.checkpoint: A table is built by adding the same number once more for every row.
items.misconception: Adding the row number instead of the table's own number, so that 28 becomes 31.

steps: So taking twelve seven times is the same as taking six seven times and doubling the answer.
6 x 7 = 42, and double 42 is 84, so 12 x 7 = 84.
items.answer: 84, because every product in the table of twelve is double the product in the same row of the table of six
items.question: The table of six gives 6 x 7 = 42. What is 12 x 7, and why?
items.checkpoint: The table of twelve is the table of six doubled, row for row.
items.misconception: Adding six to 42 instead of doubling it, which gives 48.

steps: An even number is made up of twos.
Taking it any number of times leaves it made up of twos, so the product stays even.
16 x 9 = 144, which ends in 4, and 4 is even.
items.answer: No. 16 is even, so every product in its table is even, and 16 x 9 = 144
items.question: Without working it out, say whether 16 x 9 can end in an odd digit.
items.checkpoint: An even number gives an even product, which catches an answer that cannot be right.
items.misconception: Deciding the product must be odd because the multiplier 9 is odd.

steps: The ones column needs 2 x 13 = 26, so 6 is written and 2 is carried.
The tens column needs 1 x 13 = 13, and the carried 2 makes 15, so 5 is written and 1 is carried.
The hundreds column needs 4 x 13 = 52, and the carried 1 makes 53, which gives 5356.
items.answer: 5356, in three steps, one for each column of the multiplicand
items.question: Find 412 x 13 using the table of thirteen, and say how many steps it took.
items.checkpoint: A table past ten turns a two digit multiplier into a single fact for each column.
items.misconception: Using the 1 and the 3 of 13 as if they were two separate one digit multipliers, which loses the tens of the multiplier.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Build the first four rows of the table of eleven by repeated addition.
In the table of fifteen the third row is 45. Which row holds 75?
The table of eight gives 8 x 6 = 48. What is 16 x 6?
items.final_answer: 96, because the table of sixteen is the table of eight doubled

items.question: 6 x 9 = 54. Use it to find 12 x 9, and say what you did to get there.
A child says 14 x 7 comes to 99. Why can that be wrong before you check any working?
items.final_answer: Because 14 is even, so every product in its table is even, and 99 is odd. The product is 98

items.question: Is every product in the table of fifteen even?
items.final_answer: No. 15 is odd, so its products are odd and even by turns, such as 15, 30 and 45

items.question: Find 507 x 12 using the table of twelve.
Find 1428 x 16 using the table of sixteen.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: fills the next row by adding the table's own number to the row above
keeps the tally of how many times the number has been taken
stands two finished tables side by side with their rows level
lights two rows at the same level and names what links them
sorts every product of a table by its last digit into odd and even
works one product with a table and without one, and counts the steps
opens any empty table from eleven to sixteen

teaching_notes: The page prints six empty tables on purpose, and the purpose is lost the moment an answer is looked up. Keep the builder in adding mode and make every row come from the row above it. It is slow, and the slowness is the lesson. Once two tables are standing, open the compare rail and put the table of six beside the table of twelve, then the table of eight beside the table of sixteen. Do not name the pattern first. Ask what has happened to each row and wait for somebody to say doubled. The even check is the cheapest thing in this tool and the most used: a child who knows an even number cannot give an odd product can catch a slip without redoing any working. Finish on the steps counter. Work one product with the table of thirteen and the same product without it, and count the steps both ways, because the reason for learning a table past ten is not that it is printed but that it is shorter. The closing lab is this tool with the screen taken away: problem cards at one end of the room, answer cards at the other, and a clock running.
generation_prompt: Build a multiplication table tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. An empty table of ten numbered rows stands on the canvas with only the number itself written into the first row, and there is no lookup anywhere in the tool: the only control that fills a row adds the table's own number to the row above it, drawing the addition as a visible step off the previous total. A running count down the side tallies how many times the number has been taken, staying level with the rows. A compare rail opens below holding two finished tables side by side with their rows aligned, and a light a pair control lights two rows at the same level and names the relation between them, set up for the table of twelve against the table of six and the table of sixteen against the table of eight. An even product check opens under a finished table with an odd tray and an even tray, sorting every product by its last digit and pushing an odd answer back out when the table was built on an even number. A steps counter works one product twice, once with a table past ten and once with the multiplier split into two rows that are then added, and counts the steps each route took. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Start at the number itself and add it again for every row. Do not look any row up. When your table is finished, stand it beside another one on the rail and read the two rows that sit level. Then open the even check and look at the last digit of every answer.
